units.title: Inference number formats and what gets quantized
outcomes: Explain how INT8, INT4, FP8 and microscaled FP4 trade dynamic range against storage, and where each sits in a serving path.
Derive weight memory for a dense model under FP16, INT8 and INT4, and state which tensors the count covers.
Distinguish weight-only, weight-activation and KV quantization by what gets smaller, what gets faster and what still needs high precision.
units.why: Precision sets the memory floor for every later decision. A plan that confuses nominal bits with served bytes mispredicts capacity by gigabytes.

Measure what the format choice buys on your GPU.

study.title: Day 13: number formats from scratch
study.locator: Notebook day13/quantization-number-formats.ipynb: Part 1 Quantization Math (scale and zero point), Part 2 Memory Savings and Throughput Impact, Part 3 FP8, Part 4 NVFP4

focus: INT formats spread levels evenly while FP formats spend bits on exponent range. Activations with outliers therefore prefer FP8 E4M3 over INT8 at the same width.
W4A16 means 4-bit weights with 16-bit activations. Weight-only quantization shrinks storage and weight traffic but still computes in high precision after dequantization.
Weight-activation quantization can raise compute throughput, but only where a kernel for the exact pair exists on your GPU. A format without kernel support is storage only.
KV quantization targets capacity and decode traffic, not prefill FLOPs. Without a quantized attention kernel the values are dequantized back before the dot product.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive that a 7B-parameter model needs 14 GB in FP16, 7 GB in INT8 and 3.5 GB in INT4 for weights alone, then name the two costs the nominal count omits: per-group scales with zero points, and the KV cache.
traps: Reading H100 FP8 throughput as a portable speedup. FP8 Tensor Core rates need Hopper or newer hardware; on older hardware that path does not exist.
Counting 4 bits per weight. Group scales, zero points and alignment push the served rate above nominal; NVFP4 lands near 4.5 effective bits per weight.
Expecting KV quantization to cut prefill time. It cuts capacity and decode traffic; a latency win needs a quantized attention kernel alongside it.

selfTest.q: A 7B model needs 14 GB for weights in FP16. What do INT8 and INT4 need, and what is missing from both numbers?
selfTest.a: 7 GB and 3.5 GB. Both omit scale and zero-point storage, alignment padding, and the KV cache and activations.

selfTest.q: Why does FP8 E4M3 suit spiky activations better than INT8 at the same width?
selfTest.a: Its exponent bits give wide dynamic range for outlier magnitudes. INT8 spreads levels evenly, so one scale either saturates on the outlier or crushes small values.

selfTest.q: A weight-only INT4 model shows slower first-token latency than the FP16 baseline at high concurrency. What mechanism explains it?
selfTest.a: Weights are dequantized to 16-bit before compute, so prefill arithmetic does not shrink while dequantization overhead is added. Weight-only quantization buys memory and decode bandwidth, not compute.

selfTest.q: The KV cache is quantized but attention still runs in FP16. What happens each step?
selfTest.a: Values are dequantized back before the dot product. Capacity falls but arithmetic cost does not; keep this separate from a quantized-attention speedup.

units.title: Symmetric and asymmetric quantization, scales, zero points and granularity
outcomes: Derive symmetric and asymmetric quantize and dequantize maps, with scale, zero point and clipping.
Compute representable range and worst-case rounding error for a stated width and granularity.

units.why: Every quantized serving path is this map plus metadata. If you cannot predict what a scale does to small values, calibration and method comparisons stay mysterious.

study.title: Quantization preliminaries: symmetry, static versus dynamic, granularity
study.locator: SmoothQuant arXiv:2211.10438v1, Section 2 Preliminaries: symmetric versus asymmetric cases with zero point, static versus dynamic quantization, and per-tensor, per-token, per-channel and group-wise granularity

study.title: Granularity: tensor, channel and block scales
study.locator: Section 5.1.1, Number Formats: the Granularity paragraphs (tensor single scale, channel per-vector, block of N values) and the MXFP8, MXFP4 and NVFP4 block sizes

focus: Symmetric maps \(x_q = \mathrm{round}(x / s)\) with \(s = \max|x| / (2^{b-1} - 1)\) and zero point 0. Asymmetric maps use \(s = (x_{\max} - x_{\min}) / (2^b - 1)\) with \(z = \mathrm{round}(-x_{\min} / s)\), rounded and clamped to range.
One outlier stretches \(s\) and crushes the bulk: every value below \(s/2\) rounds to zero. Clipping the range trades saturation error against rounding error.
Finer granularity lowers error but adds scale storage. Group-128 INT4 with FP16 scale and zero point adds \((16 + 16) / 128 = 0.25\) bits per weight.
Weights normally take per-channel or grouped scales while activations take per-tensor static or per-token dynamic scales, because activation ranges move with the input.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement symmetric and asymmetric INT8 quantize and dequantize. On \([-3.0, 0.1, 100.0]\), show one group gives \(s \approx 0.79\) and maps 0.1 to 0, then split into two groups and show 0.1 survives.
traps: Leaving the zero point unrounded or unclamped. It must be an integer code in range, not a float; otherwise dequantization shifts every value.
Quoting nominal width as served width. Scales, zero points and alignment padding are real bytes; state effective bits per value.
Copying per-channel scales to activations. Activation ranges depend on the input, so static per-channel activation scales go stale while per-token dynamic scales track them.

selfTest.q: What are the symmetric INT8 scale and codes for \(\max|x| = 100\)?
selfTest.a: Scale \(s = 100 / 127 \approx 0.79\). Then 100 maps to 127 and dequantizes to 100.0, and any value below about 0.39 maps to 0.

selfTest.q: For range \([-3, 100]\) in asymmetric INT8, what are the scale and zero point?
selfTest.a: Scale \(s = 103 / 255 \approx 0.40\) and zero point \(z = \mathrm{round}(3 / s) = 7\). Zero is representable exactly, unlike in the symmetric map.

selfTest.q: Why does one outlier destroy small values under a per-tensor scale?
selfTest.a: The outlier sets \(s\), so the step dwarfs small magnitudes. Splitting the range into groups or channels gives the bulk its own smaller step.

selfTest.q: Group-128 INT4 stores an FP16 scale and an FP16 zero point per group. What is the overhead?
selfTest.a: \(32 / 128 = 0.25\) bits per weight, so the served rate is about 4.25 bits per weight before alignment.
